titleEn: Weed control, disease, and drainage are top pain points for farmers in 2026, says Grand Farm
titleZh: 2026年农民最头疼的三大问题：除草剂抗性、病害识别与排水不畅
summaryZh: 美国农业创新中心Grand Farm发布《上中西部区域农业痛点报告》，指出2026年农民面临的最大挑战是除草剂抗性导致的除草失效、病虫害识别滞后以及土壤排水不良。报告强调创新必须基于实际需求，而非盲目追逐技术。Grand Farm通过其创新园区和USDA合作项目，致力于筛选和验证真正有用的农业技术，并指出农业已进入需要多种创新协同作战的时代。
featuredReason: 本文揭示了2026年农业领域最紧迫的痛点，为智慧畜牧行业提供了技术创新的方向参考，尤其是精准农业和自动化在应对除草剂抗性、病害识别和排水问题上的应用，对跨领域技术整合具有启发意义。
contentFull:
“Innovation has to start with listening,” says Dr. William Aderholdt, executive director of US-based agtech innovation hub Grand Farm.

Agriculture doesn’t need “innovation for its own sake” but practical tools “grounded in the conditions growers are actually working in,” he wrote in his introduction to the recent Upper Midwest Regional Agriculture Pain Point Report outlining farmers’ biggest challenges.

A greater understanding of those challenges—such as herbicide resistance and disease pressure—is critical to understanding which technologies should actually land in farmers’ hands. And according to Aderholdt, there’s a lot of “noise” nowadays that doesn’t relate to real challenges on the farm.

Grand Farm’s entire mission is about cutting through that noise by providing a space to validate the most appropriate technologies for agriculture. Its innovation campus in North Dakota spans nearly 600 acres of land on which companies can trial new technologies, access expertise, and connect with the wider agricultural industry.

Dr. William Aderholt, executive director of Grand Farm. Image credit: Grand Farm
 

Farmers’ top challenges in 2026

What farmers most need in terms of innovation is driven to a large degree by external factors, says Aderholdt.

As the recent Agriculture Pain Point report noted, “new technologies are emerging faster than the problems they aim to solve are clearly defined. Without a shared understanding of the challenges facing growers, innovation efforts can become fragmented or misaligned with on-farm realities.”

The top three challenges today are a decreased reliability of weed control due to herbicide resistance, late identification of pest and disease pressure limiting intervention, and excess soil moisture and poor drainage limiting access to fields.

Aderholdt notes that when Grand Farm began seven years ago, herbicide resistance was just another topic in agriculture. Now it is “almost every commodity organization’s top priority.”

Possible innovations to combat this encompass everything from traditional herbicides to robots and tractor implements, he adds.

“We’re seeing companies like large equipment manufacturers all come out with a version of how they’re going to use an implement to detect and destroy weeds.”

While this increases farmer investment, the severity of the problem nowadays allows for such a purchase to be “a reasonable business decision.”

Other top concerns are effectively matching nutrient needs to soil variations and labor, as well as rising input costs.

The latter has in turn pushed production costs to untenable levels for many farmers in the US; many are now seeking alternatives to fertilizers or ways to optimize existing fertilizers.

This, says Aderholdt, drives the need for either precision agriculture tools that allow for better management of fertilizer applications or even the development of tools that “optimize the ability for our plants to increase nutrients.”

Image credit: Grand Farm
Bringing ‘the right companies’ to agtech

Grand Farm completed Phase I of its campus in 2024.

As anchor tenant, Precision Planting, a subsidiary of ag machinery manufacturer Agco, runs its Precision Technology Institute (PTI) North Dakota on 300 acres of the campus. Other partners in 2026 include a mix of major ag corporates (John Deere, ADM) and startups (Greenfield Robotics, Reform Bio).

Grand Farm also opened a second campus in Georgia in 2024 in partnership with the University of Georgia.

Activity is set to increase as Grand Farm rolls out Phase II of its North Dakota innovation campus, which will further deepen the organization’s capacity as a hub with onsite infrastructure that can support more research and field testing.

This year, it also became the national program manager for the USDA’s National Proving Grounds Network for AgTech. The program aims to make adoption more accessible of technologies that can lower input costs, improve input efficiency, and deploy automation in areas of the farm that most need it.

Grand Farm will host many of the pilots for this program, says Aderholdt.

“USDA manages a lot of the scientific authority around selecting challenges and the protocols necessary for testing [them] out. What Grand Farm is really good at is bringing in the right companies to these tests, whether it’s with our partners or with UGA, and then also being able to execute on those protocols in very complex environments.”

A rendering of Grand Farm after Phase II completion. Image credit: Grand Farm
‘The age of the silver bullet’ in ag is gone

Earlier this week, Grand Farm wrapped its annual Elevate event, which explores the role of artificial intelligence in farming.

Like nearly every other industry, agriculture is currently inundated with “AI-based” offerings promising everything from yield increase to labor savings.

Aderholdt suggests the industry must be discerning when it comes to which technologies it actually uses.

“Farmers are now faced with a lot of noise, and there isn’t a strong way to validate what’s true, what is useful. I can go to ChatGPT or Claude and build my next ag web app overnight. That doesn’t mean it’s going to be good or useful.”

For AI to work in any farming context, it needs to be rooted in actual challenges the agricultural industry currently faces or may face in the future. Moreover, startups and farmers alike should see AI and other technologies as one tool in a larger system.

“The age of ‘the silver bullet’ in agriculture has gone away. We aren’t going to get an amazing trait that vastly increases yields overnight or increases profitability overnight.”

Instead, there’s a combined effort needed of many different parallel innovations, which may include a practice change or crop diversity, or it could include artificial intelligence, he says.

The startups most likely to be successful are those planning to be “part of the long haul of what agriculture can be.” That means working with the industry to create solutions, rather than simply trying to sell something.

“You hear about these startups that want to co-create and have been around five-plus years now and are gaining traction,” says Aderholdt. “A lot of that shared story is that they’re working with farmers and they want farmers to be involved in the innovation.”

translationZh:
“创新必须从倾听开始，”美国农业科技创新中心Grand Farm的执行董事威廉·阿德霍尔特博士表示。

他在最近发布的《上中西部区域农业痛点报告》引言中写道，农业不需要“为创新而创新”，而是需要“基于种植者实际工作条件”的实用工具。

更深入地理解这些挑战——如除草剂抗性和病害压力——对于确定哪些技术真正应该交到农民手中至关重要。据阿德霍尔特称，如今有很多“噪音”与农场实际挑战无关。

Grand Farm的使命就是通过提供一个验证最适合农业技术的空间来消除这些噪音。其位于北达科他州的创新园区占地近600英亩，企业可以在那里试验新技术、获取专业知识，并与更广泛的农业产业建立联系。

**2026年农民面临的最大挑战**

阿德霍尔特表示，农民对创新的需求在很大程度上受外部因素驱动。

正如最近的《农业痛点报告》所指出的：“新技术的出现速度超过了它们所要解决的问题的明确速度。如果对种植者面临的挑战缺乏共识，创新努力就可能变得支离破碎，或与农场实际情况脱节。”

当今三大挑战是：除草剂抗性导致的除草可靠性下降、病虫害压力识别滞后限制了干预措施、以及土壤水分过多和排水不良限制了田间作业。

阿德霍尔特指出，七年前Grand Farm成立时，除草剂抗性还只是农业中的一个普通话题。现在它“几乎是每个商品组织的首要任务”。

他补充说，应对这一问题的可能创新涵盖从传统除草剂到机器人和拖拉机机具的方方面面。

“我们看到像大型设备制造商这样的公司都推出了自己的版本，用机具来检测和消灭杂草。”

虽然这增加了农民的投资，但如今问题的严重性使得这样的购买成为“合理的商业决策”。

其他主要关注点包括：如何有效匹配养分需求与土壤差异、劳动力问题，以及投入成本上升。

后者已使美国许多农民的生产成本达到难以维持的水平；许多人现在正在寻找化肥的替代品或优化现有化肥的方法。

阿德霍尔特说，这推动了对精准农业工具的需求，这些工具可以更好地管理施肥，甚至开发“优化植物吸收养分能力”的工具。

**将“合适的公司”引入农业科技领域**

Grand Farm于2024年完成了园区一期建设。

作为主要租户，农业机械制造商爱科（Agco）旗下的Precision Planting公司在园区300英亩土地上运营其北达科他州精准技术研究所（PTI）。2026年的其他合作伙伴包括大型农业企业（约翰迪尔、ADM）和初创公司（Greenfield Robotics、Reform Bio）。

Grand Farm还于2024年与佐治亚大学合作，在佐治亚州开设了第二个园区。

随着Grand Farm推出北达科他州创新园区二期工程，其活动将有所增加，这将进一步深化该组织作为枢纽的能力，提供现场基础设施以支持更多研究和田间试验。

今年，它还被任命为美国农业部国家农业科技试验场网络（National Proving Grounds Network for AgTech）的国家项目经理。该项目旨在使那些能够降低投入成本、提高投入效率并在农场最需要自动化的领域部署自动化的技术更容易被采用。

阿德霍尔特说，Grand Farm将主持该项目的许多试点。

“美国农业部在挑选挑战和制定测试协议方面拥有许多科学权威。Grand Farm擅长的是将合适的公司引入这些测试，无论是与我们的合作伙伴还是与佐治亚大学合作，并且能够在非常复杂的环境中执行这些协议。”

**农业“银弹”时代已经过去**

本周早些时候，Grand Farm结束了其年度Elevate活动，该活动探讨了人工智能在农业中的作用。

与几乎所有其他行业一样，农业目前充斥着各种“基于人工智能”的产品，承诺从增产到节省劳动力的一切。

阿德霍尔特建议，行业在决定实际使用哪些技术时必须具有辨别力。

“农民现在面临很多噪音，没有强有力的方法来验证什么是真实的、什么是有用的。我可以去ChatGPT或Claude那里，一夜之间构建我的下一个农业网络应用程序。但这并不意味着它会很好或有用。”

人工智能要在任何农业环境中发挥作用，就必须植根于农业行业当前或未来可能面临的实际挑战。此外，初创公司和农民都应该将人工智能和其他技术视为更大系统中的一个工具。

“农业中‘银弹’的时代已经过去。我们不会一夜之间获得一个能大幅提高产量或盈利能力的惊人性状。”

相反，需要许多不同的并行创新共同努力，可能包括实践改变或作物多样化，也可能包括人工智能，他说。

最有可能成功的初创公司是那些计划“在农业可能成为的样子中扮演长期角色”的公司。这意味着与行业合作创造解决方案，而不是简单地试图销售某些东西。

“你会听到一些初创公司想要共同创造，并且已经存在五年以上，正在获得发展势头，”阿德霍尔特说。“他们共同的故事是，他们与农民合作，希望农民参与创新。”
author: Jennifer Marston
